record.paper_title: Selected Open Problems in Discrete Geometry and Optimization
record.context_brief: Exact small contact numbers in E^3
record.original_question: For the contact-number function C(n), the maximum number of touching pairs in a packing of n unit balls in E^3, determine rigorously whether the lower bounds C(10) >= 25, C(11) >= 29, C(12) >= 33, and C(13) >= 36 are exact equalities.

evidence.quote: Finally, if we take the 12 vertices of a cuboctahedron of edge length 2 in E3 along with its center of symmetry, then the 13 unit balls centered about them have 36 contacts implying that C(13) >= 36. Whether in any of the inequalities C(10) >= 25, C(11) >= 29, C(12) >= 33, and C(13) >= 36 we have equality seems to be an open question.
The main results are: C(9) = 21; C(10) = 25 and C(11) = 29. However, the status of the mathematical rigour of the approaches remains to be seen.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n \ge 2$, consider packings of $n$ closed unit balls in Euclidean 3-space $\mathbb{E}^3$, i.e., finite families of closed balls of radius $1$ with pairwise disjoint interiors. The contact graph of such a packing has the balls as vertices and an edge between two balls whenever they touch (i.e., their boundaries share exactly one point). Define the contact number $C(n)$ to be the maximum, over all packings of $n$ unit balls in $\mathbb{E}^3$, of the number of edges in the contact graph (equivalently, the maximum number of touching pairs).

It is known that
$$C(10) \ge 25,\quad C(11) \ge 29,\quad C(12) \ge 33,\quad C(13) \ge 36,$$
where the last bound is realized by placing $13$ unit balls at the $12$ vertices of a cuboctahedron of edge length $2$ together with its center of symmetry.

Determine, with a rigorous proof, whether each of these four inequalities is an equality. That is, decide for each $n \in \{10, 11, 12, 13\}$ whether $C(n)$ equals the stated lower bound or is strictly larger, and if larger, determine the exact value.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and works by Bezdek and collaborators (through 2023) continue to list these equalities as open. While claimed proofs for C(10) = 25 and C(11) = 29 have appeared, their mathematical rigor remains under discussion, and C(12) and C(13) are still treated as open in the discrete-geometry literature.

status_evidence.snippet: Question of whether C(10) ≥ 25, C(11) ≥ 29, C(12) ≥ 33, and C(13) ≥ 36 are equalities is described as a challenging open question.

status_evidence.claim: Active research; problem remains discussed as open in recent works.
